Ceylinco Life’s approach to sustainability reflects a shift from compliance-driven ESG frameworks to a deeply embedded business philosophy that shapes how the company operates, invests, and engages with society. As Sri Lanka’s life insurance market leader, the company has positioned sustainability not as a peripheral initiative, but as a central pillar of long-term value creation for policyholders, employees, communities, shareholders, and the environment.

The integration of Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) principles into decision-making across the organisation is central to this approach. From investment strategies to customer engagement and operational processes, sustainability considerations are built into the company’s growth model. This alignment enables Ceylinco Life to balance financial performance with broader responsibilities such as environmental stewardship, financial inclusion, and ethical governance.

One of the most visible expressions of this commitment is the company’s Green Building Network, a nationwide initiative to develop environmentally responsible branch infrastructure. These purpose-built facilities are designed to operate with minimal environmental impact while enhancing efficiency. Many of these branches are fully powered by solar energy, with the ability to generate surplus electricity that can be fed back into the national grid. The buildings themselves incorporate sustainable construction materials, energy-efficient architectural design, and systems that optimise natural lighting and ventilation.

Water, wastewater and sewage management are also integral to these eco-friendly branches. Rainwater harvesting, wastewater recycling, and on-site treatment systems significantly reduce freshwater consumption and environmental discharge. These features are complemented by environmentally sensitive construction practices that minimise disruption to surrounding ecosystems.  

Collectively, Ceylinco Life’s Green Building Network represents a practical, scalable model of sustainable infrastructure within the financial services sector. At end 2025, Ceylinco Life had 32 green branch buildings on company-owned land. These buildings had generated approximately 1.12 GWh of solar energy, harvested 3.08 million litres of rainwater and recycled 1.386 million litres of water.

Beyond infrastructure, Ceylinco Life has demonstrated a consistent focus on measuring and managing its environmental footprint. The company has undertaken comprehensive assessments of its greenhouse gas emissions, covering both direct and indirect impacts of its operations. These exercises provide a scientific basis for tracking progress and identifying opportunities for improvement. The company has set measurable targets for reducing its carbon footprint and has already achieved reductions through initiatives such as optimising energy use, reducing paper consumption, and improving fuel efficiency.

On the social front, Ceylinco Life’s sustainability strategy is closely linked to its core business of providing financial protection. By expanding access to insurance solutions, particularly among underserved communities, the company supports financial resilience and inclusion. This is complemented by a range of community development initiatives, including healthcare support for public hospitals, infrastructure improvements in schools, and outreach programmes like free medical camps that address local needs across the country. More than 2,000 people benefit annually through the Ceylinco Life ‘Waidya Hamuwa’ programme, at least 50 per cent of them women. Since the programme’s inception, over 150,000 people have received free diagnostic tests and consultations with doctors.

Additionally, the company has built and donated classrooms 89 schools to date and helps maintain them, contributing significantly to improved access to quality education for children across communities.

Employee wellbeing and development form another important dimension of the company’s social agenda. Structured programmes for leadership development, digital upskilling, and talent management ensure that the workforce is equipped to meet evolving industry demands. The company has also placed emphasis on increasing the participation and empowerment of women within both its corporate and sales teams, reflecting a broader commitment to diversity and inclusion.

Governance underpins all these efforts. Ceylinco Life maintains a strong focus on transparency, ethics, and regulatory compliance, supported by robust risk management frameworks. ESG oversight is embedded within corporate governance structures, ensuring accountability at board and senior management levels. Sustainability performance is monitored through defined policies and reporting mechanisms, with increasing alignment to emerging global standards in ESG disclosure.

Innovation plays a critical role in advancing sustainability objectives. The company’s investment in digital transformation has enhanced customer experience while reducing reliance on paper-based processes and improving operational efficiency. At the same time, its participation in green financing initiatives, including investments in renewable energy projects, demonstrates a commitment to supporting the transition to a low-carbon economy.

Ceylinco Life’s contribution to sustainable economic growth is therefore multi-dimensional. The company’s products provide financial security and continuity when families face the loss of their primary breadwinner or the financial burden of serious illness. For decades, ports have been judged by the numbers that define operational success. Throughput, crane productivity, vessel turnaround time and berth utilisation have long been regarded as the key indicators of performance. They remain fundamental to global trade.

Today, however, another set of metrics is becoming just as important.

How much energy does a terminal consume? How much carbon has it eliminated? How efficiently does it use water and other resources? How does it coexist with the communities and ecosystems that surround it?

Around the world, the definition of a successful port is changing. Increasingly, ports are being judged not only by how efficiently they move cargo, but by how responsibly they do it.

This reflects a broader shift in Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) thinking. For many years, sustainability in the corporate world was often associated with Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR), where environmental and community initiatives existed alongside the business. Today, leading port operators are embedding sustainability into the way terminals are designed, powered and operated.

Rather than treating ESG as a separate programme, it is becoming part of operational strategy. Few examples illustrate this transition more clearly than Colombo International Container Terminals (CICT).

As one of Sri Lanka’s largest deep-water container terminals and a member of the China Merchants Port network, CICT has steadily integrated environmental performance into its day-to-day operations. The terminal’s electrification programme demonstrates how environmental responsibility and operational efficiency can reinforce one another.

The conversion of Rubber-Tyred Gantry (RTG) cranes from diesel to electricity has significantly reduced emissions while lowering fuel consumption and improving working conditions. The conversion of diesel-powered Inter Terminal Vehicles (ITV) to electric continues the same trajectory, showing that cleaner operations can also deliver greater efficiency and long-term cost savings.

This is a reminder that the most sustainable terminal is often the most efficient one.

The same philosophy extends beyond equipment.

Rainwater harvesting, condensate water reuse, digital documentation, intelligent energy management systems and smart operational technologies may appear to be separate initiatives. Viewed together, however, they represent a broader approach to resource management.

Waste is no longer viewed simply as rubbish to be disposed of. It includes wasted fuel, wasted electricity, wasted water, wasted paper and wasted time. Reducing each of these improves both environmental performance and operational productivity.

This is one of the most significant shifts taking place in the global port industry. Sustainability is moving away from isolated environmental projects towards continuous operational improvement.

The evolution is also changing how ports view their relationship with the communities and natural environments around them.

Ports are often seen primarily as transport infrastructure. In reality, they influence coastlines, urban environments, local economies and marine ecosystems. Their responsibilities therefore extend beyond the terminal gate.

This broader understanding is reflected in initiatives such as CICT’s long-standing support for Sri Lanka’s Wheelchair Tennis programme, which has helped athletes compete internationally while promoting inclusion through sport, and the Ambassador Cup, in partnership with the University of Colombo, which brings together students from universities across Sri Lanka through badminton, encouraging positive engagement and helping foster a more inclusive and constructive university culture.

More recently, the terminal became the principal sponsor of a three-year sea turtle conservation initiative led by the Wildlife and Nature Protection Society in partnership with the Turtle and Coastal Health United Programme. The project combines habitat restoration, scientific monitoring, community participation and public education to protect an important urban coastal ecosystem in Colombo.

Viewed independently, these may appear to be conventional CSR projects. Together, they reflect a wider recognition that healthy businesses ultimately depend on healthy communities and healthy ecosystems.

This philosophy is aligned with the broader ESG direction of the China Merchants Port network, while reflecting Sri Lanka’s local environmental and social priorities.

Governance provides the foundation for these efforts. At CICT, sustainability is supported by clear accountability, internationally certified management systems, robust safety and environmental management practices, strong compliance controls, and the integration of ESG considerations into operational and investment decisions. CICT maintains certification to internationally recognised standards, including ISO 14001 (Environmental Management Systems), ISO 45001 (Occupational Health and Safety Management Systems). These internationally recognised frameworks promote disciplined management, continuous improvement and operational excellence, ensuring that environmental and social commitments are translated into measurable, transparent and accountable action.

The maritime industry is now entering a period in which customers, investors and regulators are placing increasing emphasis on ESG performance. Cleaner supply chains, lower emissions and responsible governance are becoming competitive advantages rather than compliance requirements.

This presents both a challenge and an opportunity for ports.

The challenge is to continue improving productivity while reducing environmental impact. The opportunity is to demonstrate that these two objectives are no longer in conflict. Modern terminals increasingly show that operational efficiency, resource conservation and environmental stewardship can strengthen one another.

Ultimately, the ports that lead the next generation of global trade may not simply be those that move the most cargo. They are likely to be the ports that move cargo most responsibly.

Through initiatives ranging from equipment electrification and digitalisation to biodiversity conservation and community partnerships, CICT demonstrates that the future of port sustainability is not built around a collection of individual projects. It is built around a different way of operating.

That may prove to be the industry’s most important transformation of all.

title: How Businesses Can Reduce Their Carbon Footprint | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 23 July 2026 14:17
-     - 15

By M Peiris

Walk into most company head offices five years ago, and you’d find sustainability tucked into a corner of the marketing department, mostly there to fill out a page in the annual report. That’s changing fast. Rising energy costs, pressure from investors, and customers who actually check where their products come from have pushed carbon reduction into the centre of how businesses plan and spend. The good news is that cutting emissions no longer requires choosing between profit and principle. Many of the most effective steps pay for themselves within a few years.

Energy Use Is the Easiest Place to Start

Start with energy use, because it’s usually the biggest and easiest target. A manufacturing plant running old motors and poorly insulated buildings can often cut its electricity bill by a fifth just by upgrading equipment and sealing leaks in heating and cooling systems. Offices can do the same with better lighting controls and smarter thermostats. None of this requires new technology or heavy investment; it requires someone walking through the building with a checklist and the authority to act on what they find. Too often, that person doesn’t exist within a company, and small waste piles up unnoticed for years.

Making the Switch to Renewables

Switching to renewable power is the next step, and it has become far more practical than it was a decade ago. Solar panels on a warehouse roof, a power purchase agreement with a wind farm, or simply choosing an electricity supplier that sources from renewables, these options exist for companies of almost any size now, not just large corporations with dedicated sustainability teams. Prices for solar and wind generation have fallen steadily, which means the financial case often stands on its own, without needing to appeal to environmental goals 

at all.

Rethinking Transport and Travel

Transport is another area where changes add up quickly. Delivery fleets running on diesel are an obvious target for electrification, especially for short urban routes where range isn’t a concern. Beyond vehicles, simply planning delivery routes better, combining trips, and avoiding empty return journeys can cut fuel use meaningfully without any new equipment. Employee travel matters too. A company that defaults to video calls for routine meetings and reserves flights for the trips that truly need them can cut a surprising share of its travel-related emissions within a year.

Looking Beyond a Company’s Own Walls

Supply chains deserve close attention because, for most companies, the bulk of their carbon footprint doesn’t come from their own operations at all; it comes from suppliers, shipping, and the raw materials they buy. A clothing brand’s biggest emissions source is rarely its stores; it’s the cotton farming, dyeing, and fabric production happening several steps upstream. Reducing this kind of footprint means working with suppliers directly, asking for cleaner production methods, and sometimes choosing to work with smaller, less convenient suppliers because they run cleaner operations. It’s slower work than switching a light bulb, but it’s where the largest gains usually sit.

Waste reduction ties into all of this. Manufacturers that redesign products to use less material, or that build products meant to be repaired rather than replaced, cut both emissions and costs at the same time. Packaging is a simple starting point — many companies still ship products in boxes far larger than necessary, wasting cardboard, fuel, and warehouse space. Small design changes here often pay back their cost within months.

Why Measurement Matters

None of these steps requires complicated plans or expensive consultants to get started. What they do require is measurement. A company that doesn’t track its energy use, its fuel consumption, and its supplier emissions has no way of knowing where its biggest problems sit, and no way of proving progress to customers or regulators who increasingly ask for evidence rather than promises. Basic tracking tools exist for businesses of every size, and the process of setting them up often reveals waste that nobody had previously noticed.

The Value of Listening to Staff

Employees can be part of the solution too, and not just through token gestures like turning off lights. Staff on the factory floor or in a warehouse often know exactly where energy and material get wasted, because they see it every day. Businesses that ask for that input, and act on it, tend to find cheap fixes that head office would never have spotted from a spreadsheet.

The businesses making real progress on this front aren’t necessarily the ones with the biggest sustainability budgets. They’re the ones treating carbon reduction as an ordinary part of running a tighter, more efficient operation, the same instinct that drives a company to cut waste or negotiate better supplier terms. Reducing a carbon footprint, in the end, often looks a lot like good management. The businesses that figure that out early will likely spend less, waste less, and face fewer questions from customers and regulators down the road.

title: The Role of Renewable Energy in Corporate Sustainability | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 23 July 2026 14:14
-     - 13

A decade ago, a company announcing it would run on solar or wind power was making a statement, usually aimed at journalists and investors rather than at its own bottom line. Renewable energy was pricier than coal or gas, and switching to it meant accepting higher costs in exchange for good publicity. That trade-off has largely disappeared. Solar and wind are now the cheapest sources of new electricity generation in most parts of the world, which means renewable energy has moved from being a moral choice to being, quite often, the cheaper one. That shift changes the entire conversation around corporate sustainability.

A Cost That Companies Can Finally Control

For most businesses, electricity is one of the highest and most controllable costs they carry, especially in manufacturing, retail, and logistics. A company that locks in a long-term contract with a solar or wind supplier isn’t just cutting emissions; it’s protecting itself against the price swings that come with fossil fuels, which can spike overnight due to geopolitical events or supply shortages. Renewable contracts, particularly ones signed directly with a generator through what’s called a power purchase agreement, tend to offer more predictable pricing over ten or twenty years. For a finance director trying to plan a budget for years, that predictability is worth almost as much as the environmental benefit.

Rooftop Solar as an Easy Entry Point

Rooftop solar has become the most visible entry point for many companies, and for good reason. A warehouse or factory with a large, flat, sun-exposed roof can generate a meaningful share of its own power without needing much land or new infrastructure. The panels have become cheap enough that many installations pay for themselves within seven to ten years, after which the electricity is essentially free for the remaining life of the system, often another fifteen years or more. Retailers with large single-story stores have been especially quick to adopt this, since their roof space often goes entirely unused otherwise.

How Big Buyers Are Changing the Grid

Larger companies, particularly those that use enormous amounts of electricity, have taken a different route: buying directly from wind or solar farms through long-term contracts, sometimes even helping to finance new projects that wouldn’t otherwise get built. Technology companies running data centres have been among the biggest buyers here, since their power needs are so large that a single contract can effectively fund an entire wind farm. This approach does more than cut a single company’s emissions; it adds new renewable generation to the grid that benefits everyone connected to it, not just the buyer.

The Limits of Wind and Solar

None of this means renewable energy solves every problem on its own. Wind and solar are inconsistent by nature; the sun doesn’t shine at night, and the wind doesn’t always blow when demand peaks. Companies serious about renewable power increasingly pair it with battery storage or flexible operating schedules, running energy-intensive processes when renewable power is cheapest and most available rather than at fixed times regardless of supply. This kind of planning takes more effort than simply signing a contract, but it’s where the next wave of savings is coming from.

Reputation Is on the Line Too

There’s also a reputational dimension that shouldn’t be underestimated. Customers, particularly younger ones, increasingly check whether a brand’s sustainability claims hold up to scrutiny. A company that highlights a small solar installation on its website while running the rest of its operations on coal-generated power risks being called out for it, sometimes publicly and painfully. Genuine renewable adoption, backed by verifiable contracts and published data, protects a company from that kind of embarrassment far better than a glossy sustainability report full of vague commitments.

Regulation Is Closing the Gap

Regulation is starting to push in the same direction. Several countries and regions now require larger companies to disclose their energy sources and emissions data, which means renewable adoption is becoming less a matter of choice and more a matter of compliance. Companies that get ahead of these requirements, building renewable supply into their operations before it’s mandatory, tend to face lower costs and less disruption than those scrambling to catch up once the rules take effect.

What makes renewable energy different from many other sustainability initiatives is how directly it ties to a company’s core financial interests. Reducing packaging waste or improving supply chain ethics often involves cost and complexity with no immediate payoff. Renewable energy, by contrast, increasingly offers lower costs, more price stability, and a stronger public reputation all at once. That combination is why it has moved from a side project for environmentally minded firms to a standard part of how competitive businesses plan their operations. The companies still treating it as optional are likely to find themselves paying more, both in electricity bills and in public trust, as the years go on.

(M P)

By the end of FY2025/26, Hemas Holdings PLC had helped collect 2.9 million kilograms of plastic from the environment, a large amount of waste that would otherwise have ended up in landfills or waterways. This is not a statistic for an annual report. It is a marker of how Hemas has moved sustainability from the margins of the business to the center of it.

At Hemas, environmental, social and governance thinking is not a checklist sitting alongside strategy. It is treated as part of how the Group grows, manages risk and creates value.

Sustainability is also anchored in Hemas’ purpose of enriching lives.  This purpose is the lens through which the Group makes decisions - not just about what it does for communities, but about how it runs its businesses day to day.

Turning risk into strategy

Climate change, resource scarcity and shifting consumer expectations are reshaping every industry. Hemas chose to treat these as strategic questions, not just compliance ones. That thinking produced the Group’s Environmental Agenda 2030, built around two priorities: responsible plastic consumption and efficient use of natural resources.

The most visible commitment under this agenda is plastic neutrality by 2030 - recovering as much plastic as it puts into the market. The 2.9 million kilograms collected so far is real progress toward a circular economy. Alongside this, Hemas is improving water efficiency and expanding renewable energy use across its operations, building resilience into the business itself.

Where profit and 

purpose meet

Sustainability at Hemas is not confined to environmental metrics. It shows up in how the Group thinks about social impact - not as scattered good deeds, but as an extension of what its businesses already do well.

The Hemas Outreach Foundation is expanding access to early childhood education. The Ayati National Centre supports children with disabilities. Across healthcare and consumer businesses, initiatives are improving health and wellbeing at scale. What ties these together is a simple truth: Hemas gets more out of its social investments by using its own expertise, products and reach, rather than treating social impact as something separate from the business.

Commercial success and societal progress are not competing goals. Done right, they reinforce each other.

The real test ahead

Sustainability leadership will not come from a long list of activities - it will come from embedding its principles into the way businesses are run, and focusing on the few things that create the most impact.At Hemas, that is the direction of travel: sustainability not as a department, but as a discipline running through the business and staying true to the purpose of Enriching Lives.
